claim: Infection with Providencia alcalifaciens killed all Canton S flies within one day of infection.
source: Infection with Providencia alcalifaciens and Serratia marcescens Db11 was lethal to the flies in a short timeframe, killing all individuals within one day of infection.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Infection with Serratia marcescens Db11 killed all Canton S flies within one day of infection.
source: Infection with Providencia alcalifaciens and Serratia marcescens Db11 was lethal to the flies in a short timeframe, killing all individuals within one day of infection.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Nearly all Canton S individuals survived infection with E. coli.
source: Conversely, nearly all individuals survived infection with E. coli and Erwinia carotovora Ecc15 (formally known as Pectinobacterium carotovorum carotovorum 15) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nearly all Canton S individuals survived infection with Erwinia carotovora Ecc15.
source: Conversely, nearly all individuals survived infection with E. coli and Erwinia carotovora Ecc15 (formally known as Pectinobacterium carotovorum carotovorum 15) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Infections with P. rettgeri, E. faecalis, and P. burhodogranariea resulted in the death of only a fraction of the infected Canton S population.
source: Infections with different natural pathogens of Drosophila including P. rettgeri, E. faecalis, P. burhodogranariea resulted in the death of only a fraction of the infected population (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Genetically identical, co-housed Drosophila given identical systemic infections experience different outcomes.
source: We have developed an experimental model where genetically identical, co-housed Drosophila given identical systemic infections experience different outcomes, with some individuals succumbing to acute infection while others control the pathogen as an asymptomatic persistent infection.
evidence: Described in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The relative probability of infection outcomes varied among Drosophila genotypes.
source: In addition, the relative probability of the infection achieving either outcome varied among genotypes.
evidence: Supported by survival data from different DGRP lines shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Exposure to CO2 for 15 minutes prior to or after injection did not affect the chance of survival relative to 2 minutes of exposure.
source: However, we found that even 15 min of exposure to CO2 prior to or after injection did not affect the chance of survival relative to 2 min of exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the bacteria (E. coli, E. carotovora, E. faecalis, P. rettgeri) had been entirely cleared from hosts seven days after injection.
source: We found that none of the bacteria had been entirely cleared from the host and nearly all individual hosts still had measurable loads of bacteria (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Most surviving hosts infected with E. coli or E. carotovora developed persistent, chronic infections.
source: In the case of the most benign pathogens, which did not lead to the death of any host individuals, a few host individuals either cleared the infection or sustained loads below our detection threshold of 10 bacteria per fly (~22% for E. coli and ~8% for E. carotovora). However, most surviving hosts developed persistent, chronic infections.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load data described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The bacterial load sustained during the persistent phase of infection was constant but distinct for each bacterium.
source: In addition, the bacterial load sustained during the persistent phase of infection was constant but distinct for each bacterium (e.g., Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The Set Point Bacterial Load (SPBL) for E. coli and E. carotovora were significantly lower than those from E. faecalis and P. rettgeri infections.
source: Interestingly the SPBL for E. coli and E. carotovora were significantly lower than those from E. faecalis and P. rettgeri infections, which also differed between each other (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of bacterial loads shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SPBL for P. rettgeri was significantly different among three D. melanogaster host genotypes.
source: In addition, we found the SPBL for P. rettgeri to be significantly different among three D. melanogaster host genotypes (Figure 1C), increasing with the size of the initial inoculum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SPBL for P. rettgeri increased with the size of the initial inoculum.
source: In addition, we found the SPBL for P. rettgeri to be significantly different among three D. melanogaster host genotypes (Figure 1C), increasing with the size of the initial inoculum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: P. rettgeri loads in recently-dead individuals were 223.4 ± 21.6 bacteria/fly, regardless of the time post-injection at which the host died.
source: The P. rettgeri loads in recently-dead individuals were 223.4 ± 21.6 (mean ±sd) bacteria/fly, regardless of the time post-injection at which the host died (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies shown in Figure 2B.

claim: P. rettgeri loads in recently-dead individuals were consistently 100-fold higher than those of living individuals.
source: These loads were consistently 100-fold higher than those of living individuals (215.8 ± 23.8 bacteria/fly; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of bacterial loads between dead and living flies shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The BLUD differed significantly between different bacterial species.
source: We found that there is a BLUD associated with every bacterium and that the BLUD differed significantly between bacteria (Figure 2C), indicating that this threshold is a property of the pathogen.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies infected with different bacteria shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The BLUD for S. marcescens was 220.2 ± 20.7 bacteria/fly.
source: For example, the BLUD for S. marcescens, which killed wild-type flies within 8 hr of injection, was 220.2 ± 20.7 bacteria/fly.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies.

claim: The BLUD for P. alcalifaciens was 224.3 ± 20.5 bacteria/fly.
source: This is lower than that of P. alcalifaciens (224.3 ± 20.5), which killed within 24 hr, but higher than for S. aureus (218.1 ± 20.7), which killed within 28 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The BLUD for S. aureus was 218.1 ± 20.7 bacteria/fly.
source: This is lower than that of P. alcalifaciens (224.3 ± 20.5), which killed within 24 hr, but higher than for S. aureus (218.1 ± 20.7), which killed within 28 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The BLUD of P. rettgeri varied significantly across Drosophila species.
source: We found that the BLUD varied significantly across Drosophila species (Figure 2D) and across different D. melanogaster genotypes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies of different Drosophila species shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The BLUD of P. rettgeri varied significantly across different D. melanogaster genotypes.
source: We found that the BLUD varied significantly across Drosophila species (Figure 2D) and across different D. melanogaster genotypes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies of different D. melanogaster genotypes shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The BLUD of P. rettgeri did not depend on the initial inoculum starting the infection.
source: To our surprise, however, the BLUD did not depend on the initial inoculum starting the infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies infected with different doses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Flies injected with higher doses of P. rettgeri died earlier than flies injected with lower doses.
source: Flies injected with higher doses died earlier than flies injected with lower doses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D) but BLUD did not correlate with the dose injected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: No significant differences in the BLUD were detected between immune-deficient hosts and their corresponding wild-type genotypes.
source: We did not detect significant differences in the BLUD between any of the immune-deficient hosts and their corresponding wild-type genotypes (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements from dead flies of different immune genotypes shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Upon infection with E. coli and E. carotovora, bacterial burdens inside individual flies decreased soon after injection.
source: Upon infection with two avirulent bacteria, E. coli and E. carotovora, bacterial burdens inside individual flies decreased soon after injection (Figure 3A), suggesting that these bacteria are controlled within a couple of hours by the host, even though they are not completely cleared.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements over time shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After injection with P. alcalifaciens or S. marcescens, the pathogen burdens increased monotonically until all individuals were dead.
source: After injection with bacteria that kill all infected hosts in few hours (P. alcalifaciens or S. marcescens), the pathogen burdens increased monotonically until all individuals were dead (Figure 3B), suggesting that the host fails to control the infection.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements over time shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For E. faecalis, P. burhodogranariea, and P. rettgeri infections, bacteria proliferated homogenously in all individuals during the early phase of infection (up to around 6–8 hr).
source: For these, we found that bacteria proliferated homogenously in all individuals during the early phase of infection (up to around 6–8 hr), but that subsequently two groups of hosts could be distinguished.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements over time shown in Figure 3C–E.

claim: The in vivo proliferation of P. rettgeri in the early phase of infection is equivalent to the rate of in vitro growth in LB medium.
source: Remarkably, the in vivo proliferation of P. rettgeri in the early phase of infection is equivalent to the rate of in vitro growth in LB medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the bacteria are growing largely without constraint in this early phase.
evidence: Supported by comparison of in vivo and in vitro bacterial growth rates shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The in vivo proliferation of P. alcalifaciens in the early phase of infection is equivalent to the rate of in vitro growth in LB medium.
source: The same is true of the always-lethal P. alcalifaciens and S. marcescens (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of in vivo and in vitro bacterial growth rates shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The in vivo proliferation of S. marcescens in the early phase of infection is equivalent to the rate of in vitro growth in LB medium.
source: The same is true of the always-lethal P. alcalifaciens and S. marcescens (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of in vivo and in vitro bacterial growth rates shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bacteria isolated from infected hosts were as likely or more likely than the original bacterial clone to kill new hosts.
source: In both cases, we found that bacteria isolated from infected hosts were as likely or more likely than the original bacterial clone to kill new hosts, although we see no difference in mortality upon infection with bacteria from high-load versus low-load flies (Figure 4Aii).
evidence: Supported by survival data from re-infection experiments shown in Figure 4Aii.

claim: There were no differences in mortality caused by bacterial populations isolated from flies with high loads versus those isolated from flies that had controlled bacterial growth.
source: In both cases, we found that bacteria isolated from infected hosts were as likely or more likely than the original bacterial clone to kill new hosts, although we see no difference in mortality upon infection with bacteria from high-load versus low-load flies (Figure 4Aii).
evidence: Supported by survival data from re-infection experiments shown in Figure 4Aii.

claim: Individual hosts separated into high-load and low-load groups over the first 16 hr of P. rettgeri infection both in the presence and in the absence of phagocytes.
source: Individual hosts separated into high-load and low-load groups over the first 16 hr of infection both in the presence and in the absence of phagocytes.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements in phagocytosis-deficient and control flies shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Phagocytosis is not a determinant of the switch between lethal and persistent P. rettgeri infection under the experimental conditions.
source: We therefore concluded that phagocytosis is not a determinant of the switch between lethal and persistent P. rettgeri infection under our experimental conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that high-load and low-load groups appear even in the absence of phagocytes.

claim: No individual DreddEP142 mutant fly could control P. rettgeri infection and all mutant hosts died with a high pathogen burden.
source: No individual DreddEP142 mutant fly could control infection and all mutant hosts died with a high pathogen burden (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements in Imd-deficient flies shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Imd pathway is required to control P. rettgeri infection and shift the infection to a persistent state in a subset of hosts.
source: This demonstrates that the Imd pathway is required to control P. rettgeri infection and shift the infection to a persistent state in a subset of hosts.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all Imd-deficient flies died with high bacterial loads.

claim: Discrete high-load and low-load groups of flies emerged during the first 16 hr of P. rettgeri infection in both Toll-deficient and wild-type hosts.
source: We infected Toll-deficient (spzrm7 mutants) and wild-type hosts with P. rettgeri and observed the emergence of discrete high-load and low-load groups of flies of both genotypes during the first 16 hr of infection (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements in Toll-deficient and wild-type flies shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Toll-deficient flies are sometimes able to control P. rettgeri infection.
source: This demonstrates that Toll-deficient flies are sometimes able to control P. rettgeri infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that high-load and low-load groups appear in Toll-deficient flies.

claim: Without exception, flies deficient for the Toll pathway failed to control E. faecalis infection and all hosts died with high bacterial loads.
source: Without exception, flies deficient for the Toll pathway (spzrm7 mutants) failed to control E. faecalis infection and all hosts died with high bacterial loads (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements in Toll-deficient flies infected with E. faecalis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The specific and appropriate arm of the humoral immune response is critical for the control of bacterial infection and establishment of persistent infection.
source: These data collectively demonstrate that the specific and appropriate arm of the humoral immune response is critical for the control of bacterial infection and establishment of persistent infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that Imd-deficient flies cannot control Gram-negative bacteria and Toll-deficient flies cannot control Gram-positive bacteria.

claim: The estimated probability of control in the model correlates well with the empirically observed proportion of hosts that are killed.
source: We found that the estimated probability of control in our model, which is obtained from the measurements of bacterial load in different flies at different times along the infection (i.e. there was no repeated measurement on the host), correlates well with the empirically observed proportion of hosts that are killed (Spearman rank correlation test: S = 3.02, r = 0.97, p-value=8.17e-6; Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation between model predictions and empirical survival data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Bacterial loads in hosts with constitutive activation of the Imd pathway began to decrease immediately after injection with P. rettgeri.
source: We found that bacterial loads in hosts with an immune system that was genetically activated prior to infection began to decrease immediately after injection, demonstrating effective control at the moment of infection (t̄cc0) (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements in flies with pre-activated Imd pathway shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Bacteria grew to acute lethality in a small proportion of individuals with constitutive Imd pathway activation.
source: Surprisingly, however, the bacteria grew to acute lethality in a small proportion of individuals with constitutive Imd pathway activation (Figure 7A), suggesting that the Imd pathway alone is not always sufficient to control P. rettgeri.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements in flies with pre-activated Imd pathway shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The effect of the immune response on E. carotovora is detectable starting at 2 hr post-injection.
source: Using this method, we found that the effect of the immune response is detectable starting at 2 hr post-injection for E. carotovora, at 8 hr post-injection for P. rettgeri, and at 2 hr post-injection for E. faecalis (Figures 7B and 5D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of bacterial loads in wild-type and immune-deficient flies shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The effect of the immune response on P. rettgeri is detectable starting at 8 hr post-injection.
source: Using this method, we found that the effect of the immune response is detectable starting at 2 hr post-injection for E. carotovora, at 8 hr post-injection for P. rettgeri, and at 2 hr post-injection for E. faecalis (Figures 7B and 5D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of bacterial loads in wild-type and immune-deficient flies shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The effect of the immune response on E. faecalis is detectable starting at 2 hr post-injection.
source: Using this method, we found that the effect of the immune response is detectable starting at 2 hr post-injection for E. carotovora, at 8 hr post-injection for P. rettgeri, and at 2 hr post-injection for E. faecalis (Figures 7B and 5D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of bacterial loads in wild-type and immune-deficient flies shown in Figures 7B and 5D.

claim: Diptericin expression was extremely low at the time of injection.
source: Diptericin expression was extremely low at the time of injection (Figure 7C, left), but a measurable induction was detected at 2 hr post-injection and its level continuously increased during the first 8 hr post-injection (up to ~100 fold induction compared to the start of the infection).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements of Diptericin expression shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A measurable induction of Diptericin was detected at 2 hr post-injection with P. rettgeri.
source: Diptericin expression was extremely low at the time of injection (Figure 7C, left), but a measurable induction was detected at 2 hr post-injection and its level continuously increased during the first 8 hr post-injection (up to ~100 fold induction compared to the start of the infection).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements of Diptericin expression shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Diptericin expression level continuously increased during the first 8 hr post-injection with P. rettgeri.
source: Diptericin expression was extremely low at the time of injection (Figure 7C, left), but a measurable induction was detected at 2 hr post-injection and its level continuously increased during the first 8 hr post-injection (up to ~100 fold induction compared to the start of the infection).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements of Diptericin expression shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At 4 hr post-injection with P. rettgeri, strong among-individual variation in Diptericin expression was detected, ranging from little induction to strong immune response, with approximately 5-fold difference between extremes.
source: At 4 hr post-injection, we detected strong among-individual variation in Diptericin expression, ranging from little induction to strong immune response, with approximately 5-fold difference between extremes (Figure 7C), which may result from experimentally undetectable differences in handling, infection, or developmental history.
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements of Diptericin expression in individual flies shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The bacterial burden in the head of a fly is tightly correlated with the load estimated from the thorax and abdomen (r = 0.84, p=8.8e-9).
source: The Imd pathway is activated and Diptericin is expressed primarily in the D. melanogaster fat body, most of which is located in the abdomen, and we determined that the bacterial burden in the head of a fly is tightly correlated with the load estimated from the thorax and abdomen: (r = 0.84, p=8.8e-9; Figure 7—figure supplement 1), so we tested whether pathogen burden estimated from the heads of individual flies could be predicted by the Diptericin expression measured from abdominal RNA extractions.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant correlation was found between bacterial load and the level of Diptericin transcripts 8 hr after injection with P. rettgeri.
source: We found no significant correlation between bacterial load and the level of Diptericin transcripts 8 hr after injection (Spearman correlation: r = 0.06, S = 4225.88, p=0.75).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Empirical variability in Imd activation is independent of variation in bacterial load at the early stage of infection.
source: This indicates that empirical variability in Imd activation is independent of variation in bacterial load at the early stage of infection.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between Diptericin expression and bacterial load at 8 hr post-injection.

claim: Differences in bacterial burden at the time of death did not explain the two outcomes of infection.
source: We found that differences in bacterial burden at the time of death did not explain the two outcomes of infection.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by data showing constant BLUD regardless of time to death.

claim: Inter-individual variation in survival stems from variation in within-host bacterial growth, which is determined by the immune response.
source: Inter-individual variation in survival stems from variation in within-host bacterial growth, which is determined by the immune response.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing the role of immune response in controlling bacterial growth.

claim: The rate of bacterial proliferation is a key factor that predicts the infection outcome.
source: We developed a model that captures bacterial growth dynamics and identifies key factors that predict the infection outcome: the rate of bacterial proliferation and the time required for the host to establish an effective immunological control.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by the mathematical model and experimental data.

claim: The time required for the host to establish an effective immunological control is a key factor that predicts the infection outcome.
source: We developed a model that captures bacterial growth dynamics and identifies key factors that predict the infection outcome: the rate of bacterial proliferation and the time required for the host to establish an effective immunological control.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by the mathematical model and experimental data.

claim: Mosquitoes infected with malaria experience high and low pathogen load.
source: For example, mosquitoes infected with malaria experience high and low pathogen load (Molina-Cruz et al., 2008), rats infected with Enterococcus faecalis experience bimodal pathogen burden (Frank et al., 2015), and even the abundance of gut microbes exhibits bimodal variation (Lahti et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Molina-Cruz et al., 2008.

claim: Rats infected with Enterococcus faecalis experience bimodal pathogen burden.
source: For example, mosquitoes infected with malaria experience high and low pathogen load (Molina-Cruz et al., 2008), rats infected with Enterococcus faecalis experience bimodal pathogen burden (Frank et al., 2015), and even the abundance of gut microbes exhibits bimodal variation (Lahti et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Frank et al., 2015.

claim: The abundance of gut microbes exhibits bimodal variation.
source: For example, mosquitoes infected with malaria experience high and low pathogen load (Molina-Cruz et al., 2008), rats infected with Enterococcus faecalis experience bimodal pathogen burden (Frank et al., 2015), and even the abundance of gut microbes exhibits bimodal variation (Lahti et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Lahti et al., 2014.

claim: Genetically identical hosts may experience drastically different infection outcomes.
source: Genetically identical hosts may still experience drastically different infection outcomes (e.g. clonal population of Daphnia magna infected by one strain of bacteria [Duneau et al., 2012]).
evidence: Cited from Duneau et al., 2012.

claim: Variation in within-host disease processes can affect pathogen evolution by modulating the within-host evolutionary dynamic during the course of the infection.
source: Variation in within-host disease processes can affect pathogen evolution by modulating the within-host evolutionary dynamic during the course of the infection (Alizon et al., 2011; Mideo et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Alizon et al., 2011 and Mideo et al., 2011.

claim: Theory predicts that variation in traits such as bacterial growth rate or host response time to an infection can affect the outcome of the infection and thus the epidemiology of the disease.
source: Theory predicts that variation in traits such as bacterial growth rate or host response time to an infection can affect the outcome of the infection and thus the epidemiology of the disease (Alizon et al., 2011; Fenton et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Alizon et al., 2011 and Fenton et al., 2006.

claim: Drosophila is a prime model to study host-microbe interactions.
source: Drosophila is a prime model to study host-microbe interactions (Buchon et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Buchon et al., 2014.

claim: Drosophila relies on both humoral and cellular responses to fight infection.
source: Drosophila relies on both humoral and cellular responses to fight infection (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: Cited from Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007.

claim: The humoral response consists of the secretion of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) into the hemolymph and the activation of the melanization cascade, both of which limit microbial proliferation.
source: The humoral response consists of the secretion of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) into the hemolymph (insect blood) and the activation of the melanization cascade, both of which limit microbial proliferation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drosophila immunity.

claim: The cellular responses include encapsulation of foreign bodies and phagocytosis by dedicated immune cells.
source: The cellular responses include encapsulation of foreign bodies and phagocytosis by dedicated immune cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drosophila immunity.

claim: Antimicrobial peptides are constitutively expressed in a restricted set of barrier tissues at low levels but are massively upregulated in the fat body in response to infection.
source: Antimicrobial peptides are constitutively expressed in a restricted set of barrier tissues at low levels but are massively upregulated in the fat body in response to infection.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drosophila immunity.

claim: Two major signaling pathways, the Toll and Imd pathways, drive the induction of AMPs in the fat body.
source: Two major signaling pathways, the Toll and Imd pathways, drive the induction of AMPs in the fat body.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drosophila immunity.

claim: Strong inter-individual variation in the outcome of Drosophila infected with a wide range of bacteria and viruses has been observed.
source: Importantly, we and other groups have observed strong inter-individual variation in the outcome of Drosophila infected with a wide range of bacteria and viruses (Chambers et al., 2014; Clemmons et al., 2015; Ferreira et al., 2014; Howick and Lazzaro, 2014; Kutzer and Armitage, 2016), which suggests that Drosophila is a good model to study the stochastic nature of infection.
evidence: Cited from multiple sources: Chambers et al., 2014; Clemmons et al., 2015; Ferreira et al., 2014; Howick and Lazzaro, 2014; Kutzer and Armitage, 2016.

claim: The BLUD is a measure of disease tolerance corresponding to the maximal bacterial load that can be sustained before the individual dies from the infection.
source: Reciprocally, we reasoned that the BLUD also represents a measure of host disease tolerance corresponding to the maximal bacterial load that can be sustained before the individual dies from the infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BLUD is constant for a given host-pathogen combination.

claim: The BLUD is an exclusive measure of tolerance and not resistance.
source: This result supports the idea that the BLUD is an exclusive measure of tolerance and not resistance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that immune-deficient hosts have the same BLUD as wild-type hosts.

claim: The BLUD provides a novel measure of bacterial pathogenicity or toxicity to the host.
source: Because the BLUD varies across bacteria but is constant for a given bacterial strain in a given environment, we propose that it provides a novel measure of bacterial pathogenicity or toxicity to the host.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BLUD varies across bacterial species but is constant for a given bacterium.

claim: The BLUD does not explain the observed inter-individual variation in the outcome of infection (death versus chronic persistence).
source: Although the BLUD is a key parameter to describe bacterial virulence and host disease tolerance, it does not explain the observed inter-individual variation in the outcome of infection (death versus chronic persistence).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a conclusion from the data.

claim: The probability of death is determined by the early phase of infection.
source: This is both an indication that the model adequately describes our data and a confirmation that the probability of death is determined by the early phase of infection as described by the model.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between model predictions based on early bacterial load and observed survival.

claim: Both sets of parameters involved in modeling the control of infection and early bacterial growth have a strong impact on adequately predicting bacterial load.
source: We found that both sets of parameters involved in modeling the control of infection and early bacterial growth both have a strong impact on adequately predicting bacterial load (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by likelihood analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Variation in survivorship is best explained by variation in t̄c when only bacteria displaying intermediate survival are considered.
source: We found that variation in survivorship is best explained by variation in t̄c when only bacteria displaying intermediate survival are considered (i.e. when excluding E. coli, E. carotovora which have very low growth and mortality rates, and S. marcescens and P. alcalifaciens which have high growth and mortality rates, see Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by likelihood analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: When all bacteria were included in the analysis, differences in survivorship are best explained by differences in early bacterial growth.
source: Conversely, when all bacteria were included in the analysis, differences in survivorship are best explained by differences in early bacterial growth (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by likelihood analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The probability of surviving infection is affected by the average time at which control occurs (t̄c), but this effect can be masked by large differences in growth rates (µ).
source: These results suggest that the probability of surviving infection is affected by the average time at which control occurs (t̄c), but that this effect can be masked by large differences in growth rates (µ).
evidence: Inferred from the likelihood analysis results shown in Table 2.

claim: Death is unlikely to be a direct consequence of accumulated infectious damage.
source: This implies that death is unlikely to be a direct consequence of accumulated infectious damage, since longer term exposure to low pathogen burdens might trigger as much damage as short-term exposure to high bacterial burden.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BLUD is constant regardless of time to death.

claim: Death occurs as a consequence of sepsis or multiple organ failure driven by pathogen load.
source: Instead, our results are more compatible with a model for death occurring as a consequence of sepsis or multiple organ failure driven by pathogen load (Baue, 1975).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BLUD is constant and cited from Baue, 1975.

claim: The BLUD is a measure of pathogenicity of the bacterium, as it represents the minimal density of bacteria that kills a host.
source: In that sense, we can argue that the BLUD is a measure of pathogenicity of the bacterium, as it represents the minimal density of bacteria that kills a host.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BLUD varies across bacterial species.

claim: The BLUD represents a measure of host disease tolerance as it corresponds to the maximal bacterial load that can be sustained in the host without dying from the infection.
source: Reciprocally, the BLUD also represents a measure of host disease tolerance (Soares et al., 2017) as it corresponds to the maximal bacterial load that can be sustained in the host without dying from the infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BLUD varies across host genotypes and cited from Soares et al., 2017.

claim: The timing and intensity of AMP production is the most crucial factor for controlling bacterial infection in Drosophila.
source: In contrast, our study indicates that the timing and intensity of AMP production is the most crucial factor for controlling bacterial infection in Drosophila.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing the critical role of the Imd and Toll pathways.

claim: Adult Drosophila have only a small number of hemocytes due to loss of hemocytes upon aging.
source: One intriguing hypothesis for reconciling the two observations is that adult Drosophila have only a small number of hemocytes due to loss of hemocytes upon aging (Guillou et al., 2016), while this might not be the case in Tenebrio.
evidence: Cited from Guillou et al., 2016.

claim: Complete bacterial clearance rarely happens in Drosophila.
source: We found that complete bacterial clearance rarely happens in Drosophila.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements showing persistent infections in most surviving flies.

claim: With all seven pathogens in this study, in no case were the bacteria fully cleared from all hosts even a week after the initial infection.
source: With all seven pathogens in this study, in no case were the bacteria fully cleared from all hosts even a week after the initial infection, even in cases where 100% of hosts survived the infection.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements at seven days post-injection.

claim: Persistent infections stabilized at a fixed load for each pathogen, the SPBL.
source: Persistent infections stabilized at a fixed load for each pathogen, the SPBL.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements over time showing stable loads in surviving flies.

claim: Individual flies would carry persistent infections for several days before suddenly dying with a pathogen burden that had reached the BLUD on rare occasion.
source: On rare occasion, individual flies in our study would carry persistent infections for several days before suddenly dying with a pathogen burden that had reached the BLUD.
evidence: Observed in the experimental data.

claim: There are some conditions under which a persistent infection can re-emerge as an acute infection.
source: This suggests that there are some conditions under which a persistent infection can re-emerge as an acute infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that some flies with persistent infections later died with high bacterial loads.

claim: The SPBL varies with both host and pathogen genotype.
source: As the SPBL varies with both host and pathogen genotype, it is presumably subject to selection in both.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load measurements showing variation in SPBL across host genotypes and bacterial species.

claim: Forcing an infection into the persistent state is effectively a disease tolerance strategy from the host perspective.
source: In that context, it is worth noting that forcing an infection into the persistent state is effectively a disease tolerance strategy from the host perspective, yet the pathogen burden borne may still carry lifelong fitness cost.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hosts survive with persistent infections.

claim: Either persistence or acute lethality may be favored from the pathogen's perspective depending on the conditions of transmission.
source: From the pathogen's perspective, either persistence or acute lethality may be favored depending on the conditions of transmission.
evidence: Based on evolutionary theory of pathogen transmission.

claim: Selection for high growth rate due to competition between bacterial genotypes within a host may trade off against the capacity to establish persistent infection.
source: Moreover, selection for high growth rate due to competition between bacterial genotypes within a host (Alizon et al., 2009; 2013) may trade off against the capacity to establish persistent infection.
evidence: Based on evolutionary theory cited from Alizon et al., 2009 and 2013.

claim: Potentially minute variations in host or pathogen physiology during the early phase of infection can have dramatic effects on the ultimate outcome.
source: With the present work, we argue that hosts are slightly more complex and that potentially minute variations in host or pathogen physiology during the early phase of infection can have dramatic effects on the ultimate outcome.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing the importance of early infection dynamics.

claim: Three parameters (t̄c, μ, nTip) are sufficient to predict ultimate infection outcome.
source: We have defined three parameters (t̄c, μ, nTip) that are sufficient to predict ultimate infection outcome, although we still do not know whether variation in those parameters is due to micro-environmental variation, uncontrolled plasticity in developmental history, somatic mutations, or other factors that are uncontrolled or uncontrollable in experiments (e.g. depth of penetration of the needle during injection, site at which bacteria accumulate etc.) and in nature (e.g. time since last meal or mating, psychological status of the fly etc.).
evidence: Supported by the mathematical model and its validation against experimental data.

claim: Small differences in pathogen infectivity and host immunological control, especially in the early stages of infection, may manifest as large differences in the outcome of infection.
source: Nevertheless, what is becoming clear is that small differences in pathogen infectivity and host immunological control, especially in the early stages of infection, may manifest as large differences in the outcome of infection.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and model predictions.
